rv.q: All of which surely helps to explain the unwieldiness of “The Sign in Sidney Brustein’s Window,” a play that we might have looked back on as an early effort if only Hansberry had lived.
It's not likely that this play will get another production any time soon nor find a finer Sidney than Oscar Isaac, so sign on whatever dotted line you need to see it.
This production makes you mourn for all the unwritten works Hansberry might have given us and wonder what she would have made of our current fractured state of disunion.
What struck me most of all in this second go-round with ’Sidney Brustein’ is Hansberry’s self-conscious commentary on art and artists, as if interrogating her own purpose before leaving it behind.
This is possibly why it feels a bit disjointed and unpolished at times.
Revivals have been rare in the intervening years, and this starry one that opened Monday at the Brooklyn Academy of Music’s Harvey Theater makes it clear why.
He is forceful when he’s not being playful.
The beauty of Hansberry's play almost makes up for Anne Kauffman's production, which feels too unsure of itself to linger or make demands.
But it is a grating snooze of a play; it ponders, meanders, stalls, and ultimately gets stuck in its own plot-free thicket of words.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actress in a Play

cn.t: Lorraine Hansberry's 1964 drama earns praise in this starry Broadway revival, with critics applauding its ambitious tackling of idealism, bohemian culture, and social issues, elevated by strong performances from Oscar Isaac and Rachel Brosnahan.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats
